The Fourth Amendment (1791) protects people against unreasonable searches and seizures of either self or property by government officials. A search can mean everything from a frisking by a police officer or to a demand for a blood test to a search of an individual's home or car. A seizure occurs when the government takes control of an individual or something in his or her possession. Items that are seized often are used as evidence when the individual is charged with a crime. It also imposes certain limitations on police investigating a crime and prevents the use of illegally obtained evidence at trial.

It is an amendment specific to safeguards of justice that is there to protect you from the government and those they empower. It has no bearing on non-government agencies because they do not have wide-ranging powers to search and seize. It makes no sense to limit someone's power when it's not a power they have to begin with.

Well, technically there are. Keeping in mind that this is within the context of property on your person. When the property is not on your person other laws can apply depending on the situation.

Nobody can just walk up to you and start going through your pockets if you refuse them. However this becomes less about search and more about assault if they attempt to forcibly search you. Presumably you will both verbally and physically resist a search from a random person. It might also fall under trespass laws (which seem to overlap with assault, or "trespass to the person"). So while there may be no technical laws that directly prohibit search, there's a minefield of other laws around the issue that make it impossible to be legal without your consent or a legally empowered civil servant who has probable cause, or has been granted permission by a judge.

Another segment of law worth looking at is the right to privacy which could likely be called upon in the event of an illegal or permissionless search. The right to privacy is not a single codified right, rather it is implied by a collection of rights, freedoms, and laws which work in tandem. This can apply to both private citizens and government depending on which laws are invoked in its name.

I'd like to also point out that "Trespass to chattels" is more about confiscation and/or destruction of property. You might invoke this if they took your food and threw it in the garbage as opposed to simply denying you entry to the theater. From a legal standpoint it's a good fucking day if they do that, since you'll not only have them on an assault to your person, but an assault to your stuff.

Law is pretty quirky stuff, and isn't always intuitive. For example, in the US spitting on someone's face isn't just rude; it can be grounds for a battery charge. Most of us wouldn't expect it to be actionable in court simply because it's not usually harmful. The law on the other hand states otherwise.

A lot of this is from law classes I took years and years ago (I don't practice law, it was a passing interest) so elements may not be entirely accurate.
